title: Research Project
transcript:
Speaker 1: Tutor: Hello, John. Come in and sit down. You’re here to discuss your research project, are you?
Speaker 2: John: Yes. I’ve more or less decided what to do, but I’d like your opinion.
Speaker 1: Tutor: Fine. You’ve chosen a topic?
Speaker 2: John: Yes. I want to look at how people use public services in their local area. Things like parks and swimming pools.
Speaker 1: Tutor: Right. Well, the kind of information you’ll get is very useful for town planning, of course. Do you have a special interest in public services?
Speaker 2: John: Not really. It’s just that I found a report in the college library about an investigation that was done ten years ago, and I thought it’d be interesting to do a parallel one.
Speaker 1: Tutor: Ten years is a relatively short space of time. What do you expect to find? Do you think things will be more or less the same as before?
Speaker 2: John: I think there’ll be some differences. For example, I think the number of people going to the library will have decreased. Tutor: Mhmm. John: And I’d guess that older people are using the sports center more often than they used to.
Speaker 1: Tutor: Fine. So those are your hypotheses. Now what sort of data are you going to use?
Speaker 2: John: I was thinking of using official records...
Tutor: Mhmm.
Speaker 2: From the management or the local council... John: ...and analysing them. They should be easy to obtain. I don’t think that sort of information would be confidential.
Speaker 1: Tutor: Yes, you’re probably right. There might not be as much information as you’d like, but it’d certainly be the easiest kind of data to work with. But have you considered using a questionnaire as well?
Speaker 2: It’s okay to get data from more than one source.
Speaker 1: John: Absolutely. It’s a bonus. Tutor: You’ve already done the module on questionnaire design, haven’t you? And it’ll be good to get experience, because next year you’ll have to do something similar for your final dissertation, on a bigger scale.
Speaker 2: Okay.
Speaker 1: And what are the variables you’ll be looking at? Are you going to look at people’s level of education, whether they have a degree, for example?
Speaker 2: John: I hadn’t planned to. Do you think I should?
Speaker 1: Tutor: Well, you might see some interesting patterns.
Speaker 2: John: Okay. And that’ll tie in nicely with my plans to analyse the kind of work people do.
Speaker 1: Tutor: What about the size of your sample? Have you got any thoughts on the number of questionnaires you might send out?
Speaker 2: John: The previous study surveyed 120 people. I don’t think I can really analyse more than 50 working by myself, so I should probably distribute about 80 questionnaires altogether to allow for wastage. Do you think that’s enough?
Speaker 1: Tutor: Definitely. I know that your project guidelines recommend a minimum of a 100, but that’s an ideal number, and you’re working by yourself. And anyway, this assignment is mainly about giving you practice in research methods. Tutor: And think of ways you can encourage people to actually complete the questionnaire. For example, to make sure that your questions make sense, you should try them out beforehand.
Speaker 2: John: Okay. That’s no problem. My friends will help.
(Note: Answers for 27 and 28 can be in any order).
Speaker 1: Tutor: Good. Sometimes you get unpredicted responses, and you have to rephrase a question.
Speaker 2: And I know that you usually get a better return if you deliver questionnaires in person, but there’ll be too many. John: But I could enclose a stamped envelope for the return post. It’s a bit expensive, but I think it’ll be worth it.
Speaker 1: Tutor: Yes, good. John: Some people say that another way of increasing returns is to make the questionnaires anonymous, but usually people put their names on anyway, so I don’t think that would make much difference.
Speaker 2: Okay. And can you give me a bit more advice about the questionnaire? Would it be a good idea to have a short paragraph at the top explaining what I’m doing and why?
(Note: Answers for 29 and 30 can be in any order).
Speaker 1: Tutor: Definitely. And don’t forget you’ll need to get a bit of information about your subjects, what age group they’re in, and perhaps how long they’ve lived in the area, so you’ll need questions for that.
Speaker 2: John: Yes. I suppose that’ll mean it takes a bit longer to complete, but should I give them my phone number in case there’s anything they’re not sure about?
Speaker 1: Tutor: I wouldn’t if I were you. No.
Speaker 2: John: Okay. And do I have to use open ended questions as well as closed questions? I know the books say it’s better to have a mixture.
Speaker 1: Tutor: Well, it depends. In this case, I’d stick to closed questions. The results will be much more manageable like that.
